6.0.0.en: This verse speaks of Solomon's plea that God would come to dwell in His house and bless it, and settle and rest in it through the ark of His covenant, which proclaims the power of God (His might) and His greatness above all gods.

6.0.1.en: As the priests stand before God, they are clothed not with linen garments but with righteousness and salvation, that is, purity from every evil, as befits being in the presence of God. Then all the pious people rejoice at God's condescension and His presence in their midst. The effect of these verses may be clearer still in the New Testament, when the priests are present before the Body and Blood of the Lord in the Divine Liturgy, and the priests together with the people receive salvation through the Holy Sacraments and all rejoice.

6.1.0.en: Solomon also pleads with God not to turn away from His temple and from His anointed, that is, Solomon, anointed by God as king, because of any weakness or sin into which he or his people may fall, but to bear with them, embrace them and forgive them. This is a beautiful humility on Solomon's part before God.

6.1.1.en: And as Solomon feels his own weakness, he pleads for God's mercies for the sake of the godliness of his father David, as God promised his father mercy for him and for his offspring if they obeyed His commandments.

6.1.2.en: Be humble before God and you will obtain His mercies, knowing that everything in which you excel is a grace from Him and not from yourself. Then God will bless you and add new blessings to you, as long as you give thanks with humility. The celebration of the Temple, the descent of the fire and the appearance of God

7.0.0.en: In this verse we see that after Solomon finished his prayer, fire came down from heaven and consumed the burnt offering and the sacrifices offered on the bronze altar, and in this way the glory of God appeared mightily in His temple. This fire means the following:

7.0.1.en: 1- God's acceptance of the sacrifices of Solomon and his people.

7.0.2.en: 2- God's pleasure with Solomon and His agreement to answer his petitions.

7.0.3.en: 3- God's pleasure with the house that Solomon built and His agreement to dwell in it.

7.0.4.en: 4- The fear of God, for our God is a consuming fire. A great fear came upon the priests and the Levites, and they went out of the temple, as will appear in (v. 2).

7.0.5.en: 5- The fire burns up sin and purifies us from it, because the burnt offerings and the sacrifices are a type of Christ, who bore our sins on the Cross and endured their punishment, that is, death, on our behalf.

7.0.6.en: 6- The fire is a symbol of the descent of the Holy Spirit in the New Testament on the day of Pentecost upon the Apostles gathered in the upper room, in the form of tongues of fire, and He founded the Church.

7.1.0.en: The priests felt the fear of God and could not stand inside the house of the Lord, since they could not bear the majesty of His presence. Thus we saw the appearance of God in (ch. 5:14) in the form of a thick cloud; here He appears in the form of fire coming down from heaven; and then, a little later in this chapter (v. 12), by a clear voice heard by Solomon.

7.2.0.en: Variegated: containing the two colors, white and black.

7.2.1.en: The people saw God's descent in the form of the heavenly fire and the priests going out of the temple, so they all bowed down in reverence before the majesty of God, and then praised Him and thanked Him for His condescension and for dwelling in His house in their midst. And they blessed God because He is good and merciful forever, as they had learned from David the prophet (Ps 118:1).

7.2.2.en: Praising God lifts your heart to heaven, so you cling to God and contemplate His beauty and majesty, and your sins and worldly desires fall away from you. Then you are enlightened and feel God in your life, and you live and rejoice with Him.

7.3.s.en: (2) Rehoboam fortifies the cities of his kingdom and arms them

7.3.0.en: Cities for defense: fortified cities, which hold out if enemies besiege them.

7.3.1.en: Rehoboam settled in the city of Jerusalem, the capital of his kingdom, which was called Judah and included the tribes of Judah and Benjamin, because they adjoin each other. And he took care to fortify many cities in his kingdom, so that they would be strong and equipped, and would not be affected if enemies besieged them, and would be hard to storm.

7.4.0.en: Bethlehem: a city lying south of Jerusalem, about five miles away. It is in a fortified position, because it is on the slope of a mountain, and in it were born David and his offspring, that is, Christ.

7.4.1.en: Etam: a village lying near Bethlehem, seven miles south of Jerusalem.

7.4.2.en: Tekoa: a city lying on a mountain in a desolate, empty region, ten miles south of Jerusalem and five miles south of Bethlehem.

7.4.3.en: Beth-zur: it lies in the mountains of Judah, 4.5 miles north of Hebron.

7.4.4.en: Shoco: it lies in the plain of Judah, fourteen miles southwest of Bethlehem.

7.4.5.en: Adullam: twenty miles southwest of Jerusalem.

7.4.6.en: Gath: one of the five great cities of the Philistines, captured by David (1 Chr 18:1); it lies southwest of Jerusalem.

7.4.7.en: Mareshah: it lies in a plain, southwest of Jerusalem.

7.4.8.en: Ziph: it lies in a mountainous region, south of Hebron, four miles away.

7.4.9.en: Adoraim: it lies west of Hebron, five miles away.

7.4.10.en: Lachish: a fortified city lying southwest of Jerusalem, forty miles away, on the road to Gaza that leads to Egypt.

7.4.11.en: Azekah: a city lying near Adullam and Shoco, about twenty miles south of Jerusalem.

7.4.12.en: Zorah: a city in the plain of Judah, lying southwest of Jerusalem, next to the tribe of Dan.

7.4.13.en: Aijalon: it lies west of Jerusalem, fourteen miles away, near the tribe of Dan.

7.4.14.en: Hebron: it lies southwest of Jerusalem, eighteen miles away, and is now called the city of Hebron (al-Khalil). Rehoboam fortified fifteen cities, all lying south and west of Jerusalem, to face the Egyptian invasions. But soon afterwards Shishak king of Egypt attacked the kingdom of Judah, and these cities could not protect the kingdom of Judah, because reliance on God is the true protection, as the Psalm says: "Except the Lord keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain" (Ps 127:1).

7.4.15.en: Rely on God, do your duty, and trust that He is able to protect you, whatever dangers or threats surround you, for He is a fortress for everyone who takes refuge in Him.

7.5.0.en: Rehoboam appointed strong captains as chiefs over these cities, and appointed for them storehouses of food, oil and wine, so that they would not lack the basic necessities of life, however long the siege.

7.6.0.en: Shields: plural of shield, which is a piece of wood covered with leather and having a handle at the back, in which the warrior puts his hand and moves it, to protect his head and body from the enemy's arrows.

7.6.1.en: Rehoboam also took care to arm these cities so that they would resist the enemy, so he put in them defensive weapons, such as shields, and offensive weapons, such as spears.

7.6.2.en: And in this Rehoboam felt secure and in possession of the tribe of Judah, which includes a vast area of land, and the small tribe of Benjamin, which lies east of Judah and adjoins it.

7.7.s.en: (3) The priests, the Levites and the devout from the tribes come to Jerusalem

7.7.0.en: The he-goats: male goats. The ancient Egyptians believed that demons dwelt in them, so they worshiped he-goats out of fear of them, and Jeroboam, who had lived for a time in Egypt, took this worship from them and established it among the tribes.

7.7.1.en: Their suburbs: the open spaces surrounding the cities of the Levites, in which their flocks grazed.

7.7.2.en: After the kingdom was split and the tribes were divided under the leadership of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, the latter set up calves in Bethel and Dan, and commanded his people to worship them and also to worship he-goats. The priests and the Levites refused the worship and service of idols, and came to Jerusalem to serve the Lord in His temple, leaving their possessions. As for Jeroboam, he appointed priests for the idols who were not of the offspring of Aaron (1 Kgs 12:31).

7.8.0.en: The believers among the people of God who held fast to His worship could not accept the worship of idols that Jeroboam imposed, and they followed the example of the priests and the Levites, so they left their land and came to Jerusalem, in order to remain steadfast in the worship of God.

7.8.1.en: May your goal in life be clear, namely preparation for the Kingdom, so that you give priority to your relationship with God before all your work and responsibilities. And if anything conflicts with God, give it up, so that you may remain in the enjoyment of fellowship with God.

7.9.0.en: God warned Rehoboam that the fortifications of his kingdom were not the fortified cities but returning to God and worshiping Him. So when the priests, the Levites and the devout of the children of Israel came to him and established the worship of God faithfully and carefully, King Rehoboam took courage and grew strong, for around him were the faithful from all the tribes praying, and he too turned his heart to God. So his kingdom was established, and he remained so for three years, worshiping God, he and the people in the kingdom of Judah.

7.10.0.en: Here some of the wives and sons of Rehoboam are mentioned. It mentions his marriage to Mahalath the daughter of Jerimoth the son of David, that is, Mahalath was a granddaughter of David. We notice that Jerimoth is not among the sons of David mentioned previously in the Holy Bible, so he was most likely the son of one of David's concubines.

7.10.1.en: Rehoboam also married Abihail the daughter of Eliab, David's eldest brother (1 Sam 16:6), and she was most likely a granddaughter of Eliab (a granddaughter is sometimes mentioned as a daughter), and he fathered a number of sons, some of whom are mentioned here. And Rehoboam also married Maachah the daughter of Absalom the son of David, who was a granddaughter of Absalom through his daughter Tamar (2 Sam 14:27) (but, as we said, a granddaughter is in many cases called a daughter), and he fathered by her a number of sons, among them Abijah, whom his father preferred because he loved his mother Maachah more than all his wives; therefore he appointed Abijah to reign after him.

7.11.0.en: Rehoboam married a great number of women: eighteen wives and sixty concubines. In this he followed the example of his father Solomon, but he loved Maachah more than all his wives. Perhaps his marriage to so many women distracted him from God, so he turned away from Him three years after the beginning of his reign.

7.11.1.en: But among the good things recorded of Rehoboam is that all his wives were from the tribe of Judah, that is, there were no foreign women among them, as there were in the case of his father Solomon.

7.11.2.en: Do not be preoccupied with the pleasures of the world, even if you have the right to use them, lest they distract your heart from God, and your falling into sin becomes easy and you move away from the Kingdom of Heaven.

7.12.0.en: Rehoboam chose the daughter of Abijah to succeed him on the throne of the kingdom, either because of distinguished qualities in him, or because he was the son of Maachah, his beloved wife.

12.0.s.en: (1) Rehoboam's apostasy and Shishak's attack on him

12.0.0.en: The events of this verse are recorded in (1 Kgs 14:22-24). Rehoboam did not continue in the worship of God, perhaps under the influence of his Gentile mother Naamah the Ammonitess, so he walked in evil and idolatry, and the sodomites appeared in his kingdom, that is, uncleanness and sexual perversion spread, and the people followed their king in these evils and turned away from God. We notice the abbreviation of the details of the evils in this book compared with the Book of Kings, because here it focuses on the line of salvation in David and his offspring, the kings of Judah, until Christ should come.

12.0.1.en: And we see that Rehoboam's aim in worshiping God was that his kingdom should be strong, and this was by the support of the priests, the Levites and those of the believers from the tribes who had returned. And when the kingdom was established, that is, when he had secured his strength, he forsook God and betrayed Him by worshiping idols, and then God abandoned him, so the king of Egypt attacked him, as we shall see in the following verses.

12.1.0.en: The events of Shishak's attack are recorded briefly in (1 Kgs 14:25-28), and we see in this verse that Rehoboam walked with God for three years, and in the fourth year he turned away from God and worshiped idols and all the uncleanness connected with them. So God was long-suffering with him for a year, the fourth year, and in the fifth year Shishak king of Egypt attacked him, Egypt being the strongest nation in the world at that time, since it was considered the first empire in the world.

12.1.1.en: And the Book of Chronicles recorded the details of Shishak's attack to show God's punishment of those who reject Him, that is, to declare that salvation lies in holding fast to the worship of God.

12.2.1.en: Sukkiims: the Arabs, inhabitants of the desert and the caves in the mountains, near the Red Sea. Ethiopians (Cushites): giant men renowned in war, who are the inhabitants of Abyssinia.

12.2.2.en: Shishak attacked with a great army, of countless number, from the Egyptians and the surrounding lands, and with many weapons, for it included twelve hundred chariots and sixty thousand horsemen.

12.3.0.en: Shishak was able to take the fortified cities that Rehoboam had prepared, because there is no power that can stand before the power of God when He wants to discipline His people. Then Shishak reached the capital, Jerusalem.

12.4.0.en: The princes of Judah who were in the cities of Judah were afraid and fled to Jerusalem to take refuge in it, so God sent His prophet Shemaiah a second time; for he had come first to Rehoboam and told him not to fight the tribes that had broken away from him (ch. 11:2-4). And here he came to declare to Rehoboam and his princes that they had forsaken God and worshiped idols; therefore God had abandoned them and left them to be enslaved and humbled by Shishak.

12.4.1.en: And we notice that Shemaiah was a prophet and a historian, for he wrote the acts of Rehoboam, as appears from (v. 15).

12.5.0.en: When the princes heard God's punishment through Shemaiah the prophet, they humbled themselves before God in prayers, austerity and tears, seeking His mercy. Then Shemaiah was sent to them a third time and informed them that He had accepted their repentance, although it was not complete, that is, not from the whole heart of all the princes and the people; but God in His compassion would prevent Shishak from destroying Jerusalem and killing those in it, giving them an opportunity for deliverance so that they might complete their repentance and their worship of Him. But God allowed the people of the kingdom of Judah to be enslaved, so that they might know the difference between their ease while worshiping God and their humiliation while worshiping the nations, under the hand of Shishak king of Egypt.

12.6.0.en: These verses are recorded in (1 Kgs 14:26-28), and we notice in them Rehoboam's concern for appearance, for he made shields of brass so that he would seem a great king, although he had lost the golden shields and had become poor and humbled before the king of Egypt.

12.7.0.en: We sense here Rehoboam's repentance and his humbling himself before God because of the distress into which he had fallen, namely Shishak's attack. And we see on the other side God's compassion toward him, for He did not allow Shishak to destroy Rehoboam and ruin his whole kingdom, but preserved His holy city Jerusalem and His temple that is in it, and gave life to Rehoboam and his kingdom.

12.7.1.en: And God saw good things in Judah, so He had compassion on the kingdom and did not destroy it. These good things were perhaps the repentance of some of the believers, the priests and the Levites, who had turned away from the worship of God and been occupied with idols, and the return of some of them to God because of the distress that came upon them from the king of Egypt. And this compassion of God was referred to in (v. 7) through the mouth of Shemaiah, that God rejoiced at the people's repentance when they humbled themselves, and gave them a little deliverance.

12.7.2.en: May you seize the opportunity of God's compassion, so that you repent while you are in this life and humble yourself before Him when distress comes upon you, instead of complaining. Return to Him, for He loves you and is ready to compensate you for all that you lost because of your sins.
